Quelles options s’offrent aux femmes viv: What options are available to women in a toxic and violent relationship? There are shelters, numerous discussion groups and workshops: so many ways to break the isolation, to talk, to feel heard and understood, to take back control of their lives, to get to safety, to find refuge.
Le plus difficile, c’est de les connaîtr: The hardest part is knowing about them, finding them and taking the leap. That is precisely the motivation behind the <l1>Marathon des mots contre la violence conjugale</l1>, which begins on November 25, 2021, at the same time as the <l2>12 Days of Action Against Violence Toward Women</l2>. The idea is to talk about domestic violence again and again, to inspire a woman who is doubting herself and plant the idea of getting help. “It’s not that bad.” “Other women need it more.” “Am I exaggerating?”
Autant de phrases que les femmes vivant: These are all things that women experiencing domestic violence may tell themselves. Before they make up their minds and walk into a support and shelter home for women, they face stubborn, deeply rooted psychological barriers. Breaking down these clichés is the fight of the dedicated support workers at Maison L’Esther, in Laval, and Maison Hina, in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, who opened their doors to us.
Elles voudraient pouvoir crier que tout: They wish they could shout that everyone has a place there, that their services are free, that you can simply come by for a cup of tea and talk, if you want. Support and shelter homes for women who are victims of domestic violence are a free service offering a roof, or simply help, to women caught in a violent relationship. Whether you are in danger, have questions, need a break, or whether you go back to your partner afterward or not, the 80 homes that exist in Quebec are open to all.

<strong>‍</strong>« Cette aide-là, je su: ‍“I’m glad I had that help. Without it, I wouldn’t have been able to stand up to my ex-partner, I would have given up. The shelter saved my life,” says Chloé*, a health care professional who prefers to remain anonymous so that her colleagues and the father of her two children won’t recognize her. She lived 11 and a half years with her former partner. The problems and the episodes of psychological violence piled up. The young mother had been unhappy for a long time, but everything intensified in 2020 with the pandemic. “At the end, I couldn’t eat anymore, I stopped answering the phone to avoid a fight,” she says over the phone in a soft voice. When she managed to leave her partner, the Montréal woman didn’t understand what was happening to her. “It’s like I was escaping from prison,” Chloé confides.
Elle sait alors seulement qu’elle veut e: All she knew then was that she wanted an end to the conflict and, above all, she was thinking of her children. It was her worried mother who suggested she go to a shelter while she found a new home for herself and her children and settled custody questions with their father. From the outside, the house she was supposed to go to looked like a new prison, austere and unwelcoming. That’s because the staff can’t let anything show, to protect the women and children they take in. Chloé didn’t know anyone and had no idea what awaited her. But once she stepped through the door, a new world opened up to her, one made of kindness and listening.
<strong>‍</strong>« On leur demande : “D: ‍“We ask them: ‘What do you need? Do you need to eat? Would you like a good coffee?’” says Chantal Arseneault, coordinator of Maison L’Esther in Laval and president of the Regroupement des maisons pour femmes victimes de violence conjugale. From the house’s sitting room, the former support worker describes her work with passion. She explains that the arrival protocol depends on each woman. “Some want to take care of their safety right away, because it worries them.
D’autres ne désirent rien de plus que de: Others want nothing more than to sleep,” the coordinator explains. She insists: “The first contact is human. Beyond all the intervention and safety forms, I’m a woman welcoming a woman.” To absolutely guarantee women’s safety, a strict security protocol is applied, even at the moment of arrival, so that the address of the facility stays secret.
Ensuite, c’est la visite de la maison. P: Then comes the tour of the house. Little by little, the women introduce themselves to one another, and former residents help the newcomers. Food is provided by the house. “The women make us a grocery list; we buy whatever they want,” says Nathalie Villeneuve, director of Maison Hina in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu.
La maison est pleine de vie : on entend: The house is full of life: children’s shouts and laughter can be heard, a woman cooks her lunch, a show plays on the television, a leftover cake sits on the counter, and support workers busy themselves keeping up the building. There are children’s toys everywhere, and the walls are decorated and colourful, dotted with information about the house and tips for feeling better.

<strong>‍</strong>Au début, Chloé se sen: ‍At first, Chloé felt uncomfortable bringing her children, but her son and daughter quickly felt at home. Two days after they arrived, Chloé’s daughter turned three.
« Toutes les intervenantes sont venues d: “All the support workers came into the kitchen, and they all had gifts. The moms had made the most beautiful cake I’d ever seen. Everyone came and sang. My daughter felt like a queen!” says Chloé, emotional.
La Maison Hina, à Saint-Jean-sur-Richeli: Maison Hina, in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu. Photo: Josie Desmarais
« Il y a l’idée que les maisons sont des: “There’s this idea that the houses are prisons, but it’s just like at home! The women keep working or studying,” Villeneuve reassures us from the support workers’ office. In the houses, activities are offered; support workers provide information and are there to assist residents, but nothing is forced. That’s how women’s shelters claim a feminist approach: helping women take back control of their lives doesn’t mean giving them orders.
« Elles ne m’ont jamais jugée, on ne m’a: “They never judged me, no one ever told me not to go back to him. Finally, someone was letting me think,” says Chloé, who ended up staying almost a month before moving out with her children.
La Maison Hina acceuille les femmes et l: Maison Hina welcomes women and their children. Photo: Josie Desmarais
<strong>‍</strong>L’hébergement n’est pa: ‍Accommodation is not the only service the houses offer. “We are support and shelter homes. It’s the support that makes the difference,” insists Chantal Arseneault.
Derrière ce nom formel se cache un souti: Behind this formal name lies a little-known form of help: specialized support workers available 24/7 to listen, advise and inform.
« Tu as un doute sur ta relation ? Appel: “Do you have doubts about your relationship? Call! We’ll be there. It’s great support, because the follow-up is adapted to each situation. The goal isn’t to get a woman to leave her partner or file a complaint,” explains Kim-Anny McGrail-Larouche, an external services support worker at Maison Hina.
Pour Georgia Dib, qui travaille à la Mai: For Georgia Dib, who works at Maison L’Esther, this service is an excellent “safety net” and a form of prevention. It allows them to assess how dangerous a situation is before it escalates and leads to femicide. External services are an alternative to the CLSC, where getting psychological follow-up can take four to six months. “Our support workers aren’t psychologists, but they specialize in domestic violence, which is a specific problem,” says Dib.

‍<strong>Des groupes de discussion pour: ‍Discussion groups to talk and understand each other
<strong>‍</strong>Au-delà des maisons d’: ‍Beyond support and shelter homes, women can also turn to their local women’s centre. Among the 82 centres in the network L’R des centres de femmes du Québec is Halte-Femmes, an organization that has been established in Montréal-Nord for 37 years. Its goal? To be a place where all the women of the neighbourhood can meet and talk. The centre has become a “home port” for women in the area, a place for living and for activities of all kinds. “We do informal support every day, building bonds of trust so they feel comfortable asking for help. It breaks the isolation,” says Funmilayo Sonnus, programming manager, on the phone. This local presence makes the centres very accessible to women. Since its beginnings, the organization has offered a domestic violence support group. It is free and open to all women, whether they are questioning their relationship or have already begun their journey to heal from domestic violence. That’s the case for Chloé. After her stay at the shelter, the young mother focused on her children and her survival, between shared custody and harassment from her former partner. The months passed and her frantic life went on. On March 24, 2021, she was in front of her television when Ingrid Falaise was invited by Pénélope McQuade to talk about the second part of her documentary Face aux monstres : la reconstruction.
« Ça m’a réveillée. Ce n’était pas réglé: “It woke me up. It wasn’t resolved,” says Chloé. That’s how she ended up in the Halte-Femmes discussion group. And there again, she hesitated and worried. “I wondered whether I would fit in, whether I was too sensitive, whether my story would be judged or whether it was really domestic violence,” she says. Faced with her doubts, the group’s response was unanimous: “We believe you!” “The women seemed to believe what I’d been through more than I did,” Chloé laughs. “It’s not for us to tell them what they’re going through. We’re here to equip them, to let them make decisions, to understand that this is not a normal pattern in a relationship,” Funmilayo Sonnus reminds us. The support group gives Chloé tools to take back control of her life and prepare for her future friendships and romantic relationships. “It feels good to talk about it together, we understand each other, we discover things about ourselves,” says the young woman.
<strong>‍</strong>À notre première renco: ‍When we first met, last May, Chloé was just starting her sessions at Halte-Femmes. Still on leave from work, she was feeling better, “but not yet healed.” Today, on the eve of winter, Chloé is back at work full time. She sees a psychologist and a social worker, and she takes part in the discussion group at the CALACS, the Centre d’aide et de lutte contre les agressions à caractère sexuel. “All this work has had positive impacts in every area of my life. It feels good to assert myself, it’s a feeling of simplicity and harmony,” she says happily, joy in her voice.
S’il y a une chose qu’elle aimerait chan: If there is one thing she would change, it’s the support available for children. While hers were heard by the youth support worker at the women’s shelter, it was after their stay that they would have needed help the most. External services offer some, but when custody is shared, as in Chloé’s case, the father’s consent is also required. There is still follow-up through the CLSC, but months after her request, the mother is still waiting, and the help is no longer needed. Asking for help was the hardest thing for her to do. Today, more than anything, she wants to encourage women who are hesitating to listen to their “little voice” and, above all, to ask questions: “It’s okay to ask for help to see things more clearly. If a woman doesn’t feel good in her relationship, that’s enough.”
<strong>‍</strong>L’intervention n’est p: ‍Intervention is not the only weapon against domestic violence. To tackle what they define as a societal problem, social workers fight on every front, multiplying training sessions, workshops, education and awareness-raising. In Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, for example, Maison Hina has created two positions dedicated to awareness-raising in schools, mainly at the CEGEP, but also with community organizations, the police and CLSCs. Since 2004, they have been active and are present on all the committees. It started around 2004. “In 2007, we put together a workshop for elementary and high schools,” explain Nancy Patry and Jennyfer Bonneau, the two support workers who run the project. Projects have followed one after another since, but they are overwhelmed and would like the awareness team to be expanded. For them, “it’s an opportunity to educate and carry on the values of the house.”
